introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2026. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry TWENTY-FIVE marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) : sous-questions codées « a », « b » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou` (deux sous-questions « a » dans un même exercice seraient refusées).

Question 5(a)(ii) : le sujet laisse le choix entre deux questions (EITHER industries « foot loose » / OR couloirs maritimes), chacune de 7 marks, à l'intérieur de la sous-question « a » (16 points : (i) 9 + (ii) 7). La règle `ou` s'applique à tout un groupe de sections et ne peut donc pas l'exprimer sans fausser les questions 4 et 6 ; le corrigé traite les deux versions de (ii), signalées « EITHER » et « OR (alternative question) ».

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 6+4+4+6+5 ; Q2 8+8+9 ; Q3 8+9+8 ; Q4 9+9+7 ; Q5 9+7+9 ; Q6 4+6+6+9 ; Q7 EITHER 15+10, OR 5+5+9+6). Les sous-questions regroupant des parties (i) et (ii) (1a, 1b, 5a, 6a, OR-a, OR-b) portent la somme de leurs marks (10, 10, 16, 10, 10, 15) ; les marks de chaque partie restent imprimés dans l'énoncé. Aucun écart avec le sujet.

Défauts d'impression du sujet, transcrits avec le minimum de retouches : Q1(a) « heavy or less precipitation » (formulation maladroite, recopiée) ; Q2(a) se termine par deux points (« surface.. »), un seul conservé ; Q4 « The unven distribution » (faute d'impression pour « uneven », corrigée dans la transcription) ; Q4(c) se termine par une virgule (« sparsely populated, ») ; Q5(a)(ii) une apostrophe parasite devant « Discuss » (non recopiée) ; Q5(a)(ii) OR et Q5(b) se terminent par un point d'interrogation alors que la phrase est une consigne (« Explain... ? », « Explain THREE efforts... sector? »), recopié tel quel ; Q7 la version OR n'est pas numérotée (« OR » puis a), b)) et les parties (i) et (ii) du b) de la version OR sont numérotées « i) » et « ii) » sous « b) ». La page 3 du scan montre en marge gauche des fragments de caractères sans lien avec le sujet, ignorés.

Sujet scanné de trois pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions), filigranes et bandeaux gcerevision.com sans incidence sur la lecture, ignorés. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography 2, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2026, THREE HOURS, référence GCE26/0750/2/P52. Aucune carte, aucun graphique ni document imprimé dans ce sujet : aucune figure d'énoncé ; les trois figures déclarées (profil de sol, courbes de Malthus et de Boserup, rente économique de Von Thünen) sont des schémas qualitatifs produits pour les corrigés (origine « corrige »), non à l'échelle, sans valeur numérique.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, accords, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about », « roughly » ou « more than ». Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Question 1(c) : la description de la pluviométrie de la zone équatoriale du Cameroun (type guinéen à quatre saisons de 1500 à 2000 mm environ, type camerounais côtier de plus de 3000 mm, Debundscha à plus de 9000 mm certaines années) reprend les chiffres courants des manuels, donnés comme ordres de grandeur ; limites de la zone « au sud de 6 degrés nord environ » approximatives. Question 1(b)(ii) : barrage de Lagdo « construit au début des années 1980 » et Q7(b) barrage de Maga, SEMRY, « Opération Sahel Vert lancée à la fin des années 1980 » : dates approximatives à vérifier.

Question 2(c) : les altitudes (basses terres côtières « en dessous de 200 m environ », basses terres du Nord « 200 à 500 m environ », lac Tchad « environ 280 m », mont Cameroun « environ 4000 m ») sont des ordres de grandeur ; la nature de la ligne volcanique du Cameroun (point chaud ou ligne de faiblesse) est présentée comme débattue. Question 2(b) : l'exemple de Keta (Ghana) et l'érosion de la côte camerounaise sont cités sans détail. Question 2(a) : dates de Wegener (1912, 1915) et de Pangée (« il y a environ 200 millions d'années ») sont des repères courants.

Question 4(c) : les bassins de Ndian et de Mamfe sont décrits d'après les manuels camerounais (forêt dense, marécages et inondations, maladies, isolement, parc national de Korup) ; aucun chiffre de densité n'est donné. Le point sur l'insécurité récente (régions du Sud-Ouest et du Nord-Ouest) est un fait contemporain cité avec prudence.

Question 5(b) : les actions de l'État cité (barrage de Lom Pangar, Memve'ele, centrale à gaz de Kribi, projet de Nachtigal, port en eau profonde de Kribi, régime des zones franches depuis le début des années 1990, Charte des investissements de 2002, Cameroon Business Forum, stratégies DSCE et SND 2020-2030) sont des faits reconnus mais l'état d'avancement actuel de chaque projet (en particulier Nachtigal) et les dates exactes sont à vérifier. Question 6(c) : taux d'urbanisation « d'environ 55 à 60 pour cent » = estimation récente, ordre de grandeur.

Question 7(a) : exemples cités (crues de printemps de la Red River en 1997, tsunami de décembre 2004 avec plus de 200 000 morts, tsunami du Tohoku en 2011, crues du Yangtsé en 1998 en partie attribuées à la déforestation, inondations de Douala et de Yaoundé) reconnus mais à faire relire ; le rôle de la déforestation dans les crues du Yangtsé reste discuté.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Discuss the main ideas of *either* the theory of Plate tectonics *or* Continental Drift in understanding crustal motion and the regular distribution pattern of major landforms of the earth's surface.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The question requires **one** of the two theories. The model answer is given for **plate tectonics** (the modern theory, which includes and explains continental drift); the main ideas of continental drift are summarised at the end for a candidate who chooses it.

**Plate tectonics: main ideas**

1. The **lithosphere** (the crust and the rigid upper mantle, about 100 km thick) is broken into a few large and several small **plates** (Pacific, African, Eurasian, North American, South American, Antarctic, Indo-Australian and others). They rest on the hot, plastic **asthenosphere** and move slowly, a few centimetres a year.
2. The movement is explained by **convection currents** in the mantle, helped by **ridge push** (the elevated ridge pushes the plate away) and **slab pull** (the cold, dense plate sinks at a subduction zone and drags the rest of the plate).
3. **Sea-floor spreading:** new oceanic crust forms at the mid-ocean ridges as magma rises, and the older crust moves away on either side (the sea floor is youngest at the ridge and gets older away from it). Crust is destroyed at the subduction zones, so the total area of the crust stays constant.
4. Most of the geological activity occurs at the **plate boundaries**:
   - **Divergent (constructive) boundaries**: plates move apart, forming ocean ridges (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge) and rift valleys on land (the East African Rift), with volcanoes and shallow earthquakes.
   - **Convergent (destructive) boundaries**: plates move together. *Oceanic-continental*: the dense oceanic plate is subducted under the continent, forming a deep-sea trench and **fold mountains** with volcanoes (the Andes and the Peru-Chile trench). *Oceanic-oceanic*: island arcs and trenches (Japan, the Mariana trench). *Continental-continental*: no subduction but collision and intense folding (the Himalayas, the Alps).
   - **Transform (conservative) boundaries**: plates slide past each other, with strong earthquakes but little volcanism (the San Andreas fault).
5. **Hot spots** within plates (Hawaii) produce chains of volcanoes as the plate moves above a fixed plume. The Cameroon volcanic line (Mount Cameroon, active in recent decades) is a chain of volcanoes whose exact origin is still debated (hot spot or a line of weakness in the crust).

**How the theory explains crustal motion and the regular pattern of landforms**

- The **young fold mountain belts** (Alpine-Himalayan belt, the Rockies-Andes chain) and the **volcanoes and earthquakes** (the Pacific **Ring of Fire**) are not scattered at random but lie in narrow belts along the plate margins; the **oceanic ridges and trenches** form linear features at divergent and convergent margins; the **rift valleys** are found on the stretched parts of continents.
- The old, stable **shields** (African, Canadian, Australian) lie in the interiors of the plates.

**Evidence:** the jigsaw fit of the coasts of Africa and South America; the same fossils (the reptile Mesosaurus, the plant Glossopteris) and the same rock sequences on continents now far apart; glacial deposits of the same age in the southern continents; palaeomagnetism (stripes of rock magnetised in alternating directions, symmetrical about the ridges); the age of the ocean floor; the distribution of earthquake and volcanic belts.

**Continental drift (alternative choice).** Alfred Wegener (1912, developed in 1915) proposed that all the continents were once joined in a single supercontinent, **Pangaea**, which broke up about 200 million years ago and whose pieces drifted apart (Laurasia and Gondwanaland first). His evidence was the fit of the continents, the fossils, the rocks and the ancient climates (coal in Antarctica, glaciation in India and Africa). The theory was **rejected for a long time because Wegener could not explain the force** that moved the continents; sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics supplied the mechanism in the 1960s.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Explain any TWO causes of coastal or shoreline retreat and TWO efforts made by man to protect the coastline.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Coastal (shoreline) retreat** is the landward movement of the coastline caused by erosion that removes more material than is deposited.

**TWO causes (4 marks)**

1. **Wave erosion.** Strong, destructive waves, driven by storms and a long fetch, attack the shore by **hydraulic action** (the force of water and compressed air in cracks), **abrasion** (the load of sand and pebbles thrown against the cliff), **attrition** and **solution**. On coasts of weak rock (clay, sand, unconsolidated sediments) the cliffs and beaches are cut back quickly (the Holderness coast in eastern England retreats fast). Storm surges and high tides add to the effect.
2. **Rise in sea level and subsidence.** The warming of the earth makes the oceans expand and melts land ice, so the sea level rises and the waves attack higher up the shore; low-lying coasts, deltas and sandy coasts are submerged or eroded (the Niger delta and Pacific atolls). Local subsidence of the land has the same effect.
3. (Human causes, acceptable as a cause) **Interference with the sediment supply:** sand mining on beaches and rivers, dams that trap the sediments, harbour walls and jetties that stop the longshore drift and starve the downdrift beaches; destruction of **mangroves** and dunes that protect the shore. This is a problem on parts of the coast of Cameroon and other West African coasts.

**TWO efforts made by man to protect the coastline (4 marks)**

1. **Hard engineering:** **sea walls** (a vertical or curved wall that reflects the waves), **groynes** (walls built at right angles to the shore to trap sand moved by longshore drift and build up the beach), **revetments and rip-rap** (sloping barriers or piles of large rocks that absorb the energy of waves) and **offshore breakwaters**. They give strong and immediate protection but are expensive, and they can increase erosion downdrift. Example: the sea defences at Keta in Ghana, and sea walls in the Netherlands and Japan.
2. **Soft engineering:** **beach nourishment** (pumping or trucking sand onto the beach), **dune stabilisation** by planting marram grass or other plants, and the replanting and protection of **mangrove forests**, which absorb wave energy and trap sediment; **managed retreat** (allowing the sea to flood low-value land) and strict control of sand mining and of building near the shore.

Each effort should be explained by saying how it reduces the energy of the waves or the loss of sediment.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Compare the relief of the Coastal Lowlands with that of the Northern Lowlands of Cameroon.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Cameroon has several relief regions. Both the **Coastal Lowlands** (the Atlantic coastal plain in the south-west, around Douala and Kribi) and the **Northern Lowlands** (the Benue Plains and the Chad Basin in the north) are low-lying, but they differ in height, origin and features.

**Similarities**

- Both are **low-lying and mostly flat or gently undulating** compared with the highlands of the Adamawa and the West, and both lie on **sedimentary** deposits.
- Both have **broad flood plains and swampy or flooded areas** (the mangrove swamps in the south; the seasonally flooded Logone plain in the north), and are crossed by rivers that carry sediments.
- Both are interrupted locally by higher ground (Mount Cameroon on the coast; inselbergs and the Mandara foothills in the north).

**Differences**

| Point | Coastal Lowlands | Northern Lowlands |
|---|---|---|
| **Altitude** | Generally low, mostly below about 200 m, descending to sea level | Higher in absolute terms, about 200 to 500 m, falling gently towards Lake Chad (roughly 280 m) |
| **Position** | Along the Atlantic Ocean, a narrow strip | Far from the sea, in the interior (Benue valley and Lake Chad basin) |
| **Origin** | Marine and river deposits (sediments of the Douala basin) with recent volcanic features along the Cameroon volcanic line | Sedimentary infilling of the Benue trough and of the Chad basin (river and lake deposits), on an old basement |
| **Main relief features** | Beaches, sandbars, **estuaries and creeks** (the Wouri estuary, the Rio del Rey), **mangrove swamps**, lagoons and low cliffs; rapids and falls where the rivers drop to the sea (Edea falls on the Sanaga, Lobe falls near Kribi); the volcano **Mount Cameroon** (about 4000 m) rising abruptly beside the sea | A very **flat plain** with **inselbergs** and isolated hills, **mayos** (seasonal rivers), wide **flood plains** (the yaere) with clay soils, sand dunes near Lake Chad and the Mandara Mountains at the edge |
| **Drainage** | Many short, permanent rivers that flow west or south-west into the Atlantic (Wouri, Sanaga, Nyong, Ntem) | Interior drainage to Lake Chad (Logone and Chari) and the Benue flowing to the Niger; many rivers are seasonal |
| **Relief variety** | Varied, with sea, swamp, volcano and plateau edge | Monotonous and flat, with local inselbergs |

**Conclusion.** The Coastal Lowlands are a low, wet, indented coastal plain shaped by the sea, estuaries and volcanic activity, while the Northern Lowlands are a vast, flat interior plain of river and lake sediments, with inselbergs, seasonal rivers and a large lake.
